questions.stem: The right to adequate housing is recognised as part of the right to an adequate standard of living in Article 11 of the:
options: Charter of the United Nations signed at San Francisco
International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights
International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights
International Convention on the Elimination of Racial Discrimination
questions.explanation: Article 11 of the ICESCR, like Article 25 of the UDHR, includes housing in the right to an adequate standard of living. Australia has ratified the ICESCR, but the right is not directly enforceable in Australian courts without legislation.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes Australia's obligation to provide shelter?
options: State governments must by law provide a public housing property to anyone who applies within a set number of days
Australia has no obligations of any kind about housing because it has not ratified any relevant international treaty
Australia has international obligations to work towards adequate housing, but no person has a general legal right to be housed
Every Australian has a constitutional right to a home, which the High Court enforces against the Commonwealth
questions.explanation: Economic and social rights such as housing are realised progressively through policy and funding, not as rights individuals can enforce in court. The Constitution contains no right to housing.

questions.stem: Which form of property ownership involves owning a lot, such as an apartment, together with a share of common property managed by an owners corporation?
options: Native title
Crown leasehold
Strata title
Old system title
questions.explanation: Under NSW strata law, owners hold their own lot and share ownership of common property such as foyers and gardens, managed by an owners corporation. Old system title is the older deeds-based form of title.

questions.stem: Ana and Ben own a house as joint tenants. Ben dies leaving a will that gives everything to his brother. What happens to Ben's interest in the house?
options: It is divided equally between Ana and Ben's brother
It passes to the NSW Government until a court decides
It passes automatically to Ana under the right of survivorship
It passes to Ben's brother under the terms of Ben's valid will
questions.explanation: Joint tenants each own the whole property together, and when one dies the survivor takes the whole, regardless of a will. Tenants in common hold separate shares that can be left by will.

questions.stem: What is the main advantage of the Torrens title system under the Real Property Act 1900 (NSW)?
options: Land under Torrens title can only be owned by companies, not by individual owners
Torrens title land can never be mortgaged, which protects owners from losing it
Registration on a central government register gives the owner a secure, guaranteed title
Owners must keep a chain of old deeds proving each past sale in order to sell their land
questions.explanation: Under the Torrens system the register itself is the source of title, which makes buying and selling simpler and more certain. Proving title through a chain of deeds is the feature of old system title that Torrens replaced.

questions.stem: How is native title recognised as a form of property title in Australia?
options: Under the Constitution, which has protected it expressly since 1901
Under a UN treaty that applies directly in Australian courts
Under the Native Title Act 1993 (Cth), following the High Court's decision in Mabo (No 2)
Under the Real Property Act 1900 (NSW), which first recognised it at federation
questions.explanation: Mabo v Queensland (No 2) (1992) recognised native title in the common law, and the Native Title Act 1993 set up a process for claims. Native title can coexist with some other interests but is extinguished by freehold grants.

questions.stem: Which is an example of an NGO supporting people seeking housing in NSW?
options: The Tenants' Union of NSW advising tenants about their rights
NCAT making a binding order to end a residential tenancy
Parliament passing amendments to the Residential Tenancies Act
NSW Fair Trading holding bonds lodged for residential leases
questions.explanation: The Tenants' Union is a community organisation that gives advice, training and advocacy, and works with local tenants' advice services. NCAT, Parliament and Fair Trading are government bodies.

questions.stem: When a home is sold by private treaty in NSW, the buyer usually has a cooling-off period after exchanging contracts of:
options: 5 business days
10 business days
1 calendar month
48 hours
questions.explanation: The cooling-off period for most residential sales is five business days; a buyer who rescinds within it forfeits 0.25 per cent of the price. It can be waived or shortened with a certificate from the buyer's lawyer.

questions.stem: Which statement about buying a home at auction in NSW is correct?
options: The buyer has five business days to change their mind after the auction ends
The vendor may make unlimited bids to raise the price without telling anyone
The buyer does not need to sign a contract because the auction itself is the sale
There is no cooling-off period, so the successful bidder is bound once the contract is signed
questions.explanation: Sales at auction have no cooling-off period, so buyers should arrange finance and inspections beforehand. The auctioneer may make only one vendor bid and must announce it, and a contract is still signed and exchanged.

questions.stem: Under NSW law, an agent who advertises a property at a price lower than the seller's asking price or the agent's estimate is engaging in:
options: gazumping
rent bidding
underquoting
dummy bidding
questions.explanation: Underquoting is prohibited under the Property and Stock Agents Act 2002 (NSW) because it misleads buyers and wastes their money on inspections. Gazumping is when a seller accepts a higher offer after agreeing to sell to someone else.

questions.stem: Which barrier to buying property most affects first home buyers?
options: Strata law preventing first buyers from owning any apartments
A ban on lending money to buyers aged under 30 in Australia
A law requiring buyers to pay the full price in cash upfront
Saving a deposit while house prices rise faster than wages
questions.explanation: High prices relative to incomes make saving a deposit hard, and buyers also face lenders' serviceability tests and stamp duty. No law bans young people from borrowing or owning apartments.

questions.stem: In NSW, the main legislation governing the relationship between landlords and residential tenants is the:
options: Residential Tenancies Act 2010
Real Property Act 1900
Conveyancing Act 1919
Boarding Houses Act 2012 (NSW)
questions.explanation: The Residential Tenancies Act 2010 (NSW) sets out rights and duties under residential tenancy agreements, such as bonds, repairs, rent increases and ending a tenancy. The Real Property Act deals with Torrens title.

questions.stem: When a NSW tenant pays a rental bond, where must the landlord or agent lodge it?
options: With NSW Fair Trading, through Rental Bonds Online
In the landlord's personal bank account until the end
With the local council where the property is located
With NCAT, which holds it until a dispute is heard
questions.explanation: Bonds are held by NSW Fair Trading, so neither party can use the money without agreement or an NCAT order. The bond is generally capped at four weeks' rent.

questions.stem: Under the Residential Tenancies Act 2010 (NSW), how often can a landlord increase the rent for most residential tenancies?
options: Whenever the landlord gives 14 days' notice
Only when a new fixed-term lease is signed
No more than once in any 12-month period
No more than once in any 6-month period
questions.explanation: Rent increases for most tenancies are limited to once every 12 months, and written notice is required. Tenants who believe an increase is excessive can apply to NCAT.

questions.stem: Since 19 May 2025, what must a NSW landlord generally have in order to end a residential tenancy?
options: Nothing beyond giving 30 days' written notice, because landlords can end any tenancy for no reason at any time
A written statement from the local council that the property will no longer be used as a dwelling
The written consent of the tenant, because tenants now hold a permanent right to stay in the premises
A reason permitted under the Act, such as selling the property, major renovations or a breach by the tenant
questions.explanation: The Residential Tenancies Amendment Act 2024 ended no-grounds terminations for both periodic and fixed-term agreements, improving security of tenure. Landlords may still end tenancies for listed reasons, which critics say can be misused.

questions.stem: Which statement about the condition report for a residential tenancy in NSW is correct?
options: It is completed by NCAT at the end of the tenancy to decide what the landlord owes
It lists the rent the landlord can charge for the next three years of the tenancy
It records the state of the premises at the start, which helps settle disputes over the bond
It is optional and has no role in deciding whether the tenant gets the bond back
questions.explanation: The condition report is completed at the start of the tenancy and compared with the premises at the end. It is key evidence if the landlord claims part of the bond for damage beyond fair wear and tear.

questions.stem: A landlord refuses to rent a flat to an applicant because of her race. Under which NSW Act could she complain?
options: Real Property Act 1900
Anti-Discrimination Act 1977
Residential Tenancies Act 2010
Strata Schemes Management Act 2015
questions.explanation: The Anti-Discrimination Act 1977 (NSW) makes discrimination in the provision of accommodation unlawful on grounds such as race, sex and disability. Complaints go to Anti-Discrimination NSW and may be referred to NCAT.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the challenge of security of tenure for renters in NSW?
options: Tenants are free to change the locks and renovate the property without the landlord's consent at any time
Tenants may have to move often due to short leases and rising rents, which disrupts work, schooling and community ties
Tenants cannot be required to leave a property for any reason at all once they have lived there for more than one year
Tenants are guaranteed a lease of at least ten years under the Residential Tenancies Act, so moving is rare
questions.explanation: Security of tenure is about how confident renters can be of staying in their home. Even after the end of no-grounds evictions, short fixed terms and rent increases can force moves, especially for low-income households.

questions.stem: Two neighbours disagree about who should pay for a new dividing fence. Which is the most suitable first step under NSW law?
options: An appeal to the NSW Court of Appeal
An urgent application to the High Court of Australia
Free mediation through a Community Justice Centre
A jury trial in the District Court of NSW
questions.explanation: Under the Dividing Fences Act 1991 (NSW), neighbours usually share fencing costs, and Community Justice Centres offer free mediation. If mediation fails, the Local Court can make orders about fencing.

questions.stem: Which tribunal hears most residential tenancy and strata disputes in NSW?
options: The Industrial Relations Commission of NSW
The Administrative Review Tribunal
NCAT's Consumer and Commercial Division
The Land and Environment Court
questions.explanation: The NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal resolves tenancy and strata disputes cheaply and informally, usually without lawyers. Strata disputes generally must go to mediation through NSW Fair Trading first.

questions.stem: Which is the main advantage of NCAT for tenants in dispute with a landlord?
options: It is low-cost and informal, and parties usually represent themselves
It always requires both sides to hire a barrister before the first hearing
It hears cases before a jury, which ensures community values apply
It can only hear disputes that involve more than one million dollars
questions.explanation: NCAT's fees are low and its procedures are simpler than a court's, which improves access to justice. Parties generally need permission to be legally represented in tenancy matters.

questions.stem: Which is the most significant challenge to accessing justice in residential property disputes?
options: Tenancy disputes must be resolved by a jury, so hearings often take several years to be completed in NSW
Many tenants do not know their rights or fear retaliation, and language barriers can make the process harder to use
Property disputes can be heard only by the High Court, which costs more than most parties are able to afford
No organisation in NSW gives free advice to tenants, so every tenant must pay for a private lawyer to take any action
questions.explanation: Barriers include complexity, lack of awareness, fear of being forced out and limited English. Free services such as tenants' advice services and Legal Aid help, but demand exceeds supply.

questions.stem: An owner in a strata building wants to challenge a by-law made by the owners corporation. What is the usual process?
options: Mediation through NSW Fair Trading, then an application to NCAT if it fails
A direct appeal to the High Court on the validity of the by-law
A complaint to the police, who will decide if the by-law is valid
A petition to the local council, which can cancel strata by-laws
questions.explanation: Under the Strata Schemes Management Act 2015 (NSW), most strata disputes must first go to Fair Trading mediation before NCAT will hear them. This encourages cheap and cooperative resolution.

questions.stem: Housing affordability is best described as:
options: the share of homes that are owned rather than rented
the relationship between housing costs and household income
the total number of homes built in Australia each year
the average floor size of new homes built in the major cities
questions.explanation: Affordability compares housing costs, such as rent or mortgage repayments, with income. A common benchmark is that households in the lowest 40 per cent of incomes paying more than 30 per cent of income on housing are in housing stress.

questions.stem: Which factor is most often identified as a supply-side cause of poor housing affordability?
options: A legal ban on building apartments higher than three storeys in every state
A fall in population growth, leaving many homes empty across the cities
Too few new homes built in areas of high demand, partly due to planning delays
Too many new homes built in the cities, causing prices to rise rapidly each year
questions.explanation: When the supply of homes does not keep up with population and household growth, prices and rents rise. Governments have responded with planning reforms and housing targets.

questions.stem: What is social housing?
options: Housing that is bought by investors under a negative gearing arrangement with their banks
Housing built only for temporary workers in mining and agricultural regions
Public and community housing provided at below-market rent for people on low incomes
Housing that is shared by several unrelated adults who split the cost of the rent
questions.explanation: Social housing includes public housing managed by government and community housing run by not-for-profit providers, with rent generally set as a share of household income. Long waiting lists show demand far exceeds supply.

questions.stem: Which statement best evaluates the need for more social housing in NSW?
options: Social housing is provided only to people who own another home, so it does little for low-income households
Social housing provides security for low-income households, but long waiting lists show supply falls short of need
Social housing is no longer needed in NSW because private rents are now affordable for all of its low-income households
Social housing is available to any applicant within a week, so it already meets the needs of everyone eligible
questions.explanation: Social housing offers affordable rent and long-term security, but tens of thousands of households wait for it, often for years. This is why governments have committed to building more social and affordable homes.

questions.stem: The Housing Australia Future Fund, established by the Commonwealth in 2023, is mainly designed to:
options: fund the construction of new social and affordable housing
give every first home buyer a cash grant to buy a home
cap rents across Australia at a set percentage of tenants' income
abolish stamp duty on all home purchases in every state
questions.explanation: The fund invests money and uses the returns to finance new social and affordable homes. Rent caps and stamp duty are matters for state governments.

questions.stem: Which is a government measure aimed at helping first home buyers overcome the deposit barrier?
options: A rule that sellers must accept the first offer made by a first home buyer
The Home Guarantee Scheme, which lets eligible buyers purchase with a small deposit
A law requiring banks to lend the whole purchase price to any buyer who applies
A ban on investors buying any property in NSW until all first home buyers are housed
questions.explanation: Under the Home Guarantee Scheme, the Commonwealth guarantees part of the loan so eligible buyers can purchase with a deposit as low as 5 per cent without paying lenders mortgage insurance. Critics argue that demand-side help can push prices higher if supply does not increase.

questions.stem: Why do some critics argue that grants and stamp duty concessions for first home buyers may have limited success in improving affordability?
options: They require buyers to pay higher interest rates than those charged to other borrowers
They increase buyers' purchasing power without increasing supply, which can push prices up
They are available only to buyers who already own two or more investment properties
They reduce the number of homes built, because builders must pay the full cost of each grant
questions.explanation: Demand-side assistance helps individual buyers, but if housing supply stays the same, extra buying power can be absorbed into higher prices. Many economists therefore emphasise increasing supply.

questions.stem: Under the ABS definition, a person is homeless if they:
options: have moved house more than once in the last five years for work, study or other personal reasons
lack suitable accommodation, including if their dwelling is inadequate or their tenure is short and insecure
do not own the home they live in, even if they rent it securely under a long-term residential lease
live in a home with more than four other members of their own immediate family on a permanent basis
questions.explanation: The ABS definition goes beyond sleeping rough: it includes people in severely crowded dwellings, supported accommodation, boarding houses and temporarily staying with others. Renting securely is not homelessness.

questions.stem: According to the 2021 Census, about how many people were estimated to be homeless in Australia on Census night?
options: About 22,000
About 122,000
About 12,000
About 1.2 million
questions.explanation: The ABS estimated 122,494 people were homeless on Census night in 2021, about 48 people per 10,000; around 35,000 of them were in NSW. People living in severely crowded dwellings were the largest group, not rough sleepers.

questions.stem: Which is a leading cause of homelessness in Australia?
options: Domestic and family violence
Choosing to live in a caravan
Moving to a new state for work
Owning more than one property
questions.explanation: Domestic and family violence is one of the most common reasons people seek help from specialist homelessness services, along with housing crisis, financial difficulty and inadequate housing. Mental illness and leaving care or prison are also risk factors.

questions.stem: Which statement best explains how homelessness affects a person's access to human rights?
options: Homeless people are excluded from the protection of the criminal law in NSW
Homelessness affects only the right to housing and does not affect other rights
Without a stable address, people find it harder to work, study, get health care and vote
Homeless people lose their citizenship until they can prove a permanent address
questions.explanation: Because rights are interdependent, losing housing undermines rights to health, education, work, privacy, family life and political participation. Homeless people keep all their legal rights, but exercising them becomes much harder.

questions.stem: Which NSW Act provides protections for people who live in registrable boarding houses?
options: Residential Tenancies Act 1987
Anti-Discrimination Act 1977
Real Property Act 1900
Boarding Houses Act 2012
questions.explanation: The Boarding Houses Act 2012 (NSW) requires boarding houses to be registered and gives residents occupancy rights, which matters because boarding house residents often have little security. Residential tenancy law does not generally cover them.

questions.stem: Which is the main role of crisis and emergency accommodation for people experiencing homelessness?
options: To detain people sleeping rough until a court decides where they must live
To replace social housing as the main long-term housing option in NSW
To provide immediate short-term shelter and safety while longer-term housing is found
To provide permanent housing for life to anyone who has been homeless for a single night
questions.explanation: Crisis accommodation, such as refuges for people escaping violence, offers safety and support in an emergency. Critics note that a lack of long-term housing means people can cycle back into homelessness.

questions.stem: Which statement best evaluates government responses to homelessness?
options: Specialist homelessness services meet urgent needs, but without more long-term housing many people cannot exit homelessness
Government responses have ended homelessness in NSW, so specialist homelessness services are no longer funded
Governments respond to homelessness only by fining people who sleep rough in parks and other public places
Homelessness is entirely a federal matter, so the NSW Government has no programs to respond to it at all
questions.explanation: Specialist services provide crisis support, but advocates argue that approaches providing secure housing first, combined with support, are more effective at ending homelessness. Both state and federal governments fund homelessness programs.
